paper_title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Long-context inputs underpin exciting recent language model deployments, where the models ability to process vast swaths of personalized user data and live content during inference has led to transformative capabilities in deep research, large-scale document processing, coding agents, and data agents (OpenAI, 2025b; Gemini, 2025; Anthropic, 2025b;a; Anysphere, 2025; GitHub, 2025). When processing large inputs, like code or long documents, experts readers skim to closely read only what matters. Yet, transformers process every token of their input through each layer, whether or not the token bears critical information. The cost of this full read is attention compute that grows quadratically with input length, as well as MLP compute and KV-cache memory that grow linearly, making long-context prefill key bottleneck in model serving. Recent research proposes to address this efficiency challenge for long-context prefill through two primary approaches. First, one body of work proposes training-free token pruning, using attentionbased scoring heuristics to prune token hidden states, forwarding only the highest-scoring tokens to upper layers (Jo et al., 2025; Long et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a; Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2021). These methods are inexpensive to deploy, requiring no model training, but demonstrate limited speedups before degrading accuracy. Alternatively, large body of work instead develops architectural modifications to the standard transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). These methods offer promising prefill-efficiency improvements, but are expensive to train, often requiring pre-training from scratch and substantially different hardware and software than existing ecosystems (Dehghani et al., 2018; Bae et al., 2025; Graves, 2016; Raposo et al., 2024; Ainslie et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021; He et al., 2025; Gu & Dao, Correspondence to: lianapat@stanford.edu, matei@berkeley.edu, guestrin@stanford.edu. 1 Figure 1: Overview of TOKENGATE. (a) Layers up to prefill all context tokens as usual; at layer the gate module keeps of them, and every layer above processes only those tokens. (b) The gate module scores each hidden state with small scoring network, and top-K selector forwards the kept hidden states together with their importance scores. (c) Token-gated attention multiplies each attention weight by the gate value gj of its key, which enables end-to-end training. (d) On 2WikiMultihopQA question answering, with Qwen3-1.7B, TOKENGATE pushes the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus time-to-first-token and peak prefill memory; at 95% of the full-context accuracy it prefills 3.0 faster and with 2.7 less memory, outperforming the best training-free token pruning methods, like FastKV (Jo et al., 2025) and SlimInfer (Long et al., 2025). 2023; Dao & Gu, 2024). To bridge this gap, we ask the question, can we endow existing trained models with improved long-context prefill efficiency while maintaining strong accuracy? In this work, we introduce TOKENGATE, small, drop-in component that extends transformer-based models, enabling end-to-end trainable token pruning over long-context inputs for efficient prefill. The model forward pass using TOKENGATE decomposes into three parts, as Figure 1a shows. First, layers below the gate module perform standard forward pass, processing all tokens through each layer. Second, tokens pass through the gate module, which produces score for each token, retaining only the top-K for continued processing. Third, the layers above the gate module process the selected tokens with token-gated attention, mechanism that re-weights the attention computation using the generated importance scores. TOKENGATE reduces prefill compute and memory because pruned tokens are never forwarded through the post-gate layers and these layers never generate KV cache entries. Token pruning uses non-differentiable top-K operator, which presents challenge for end-to-end learning. We introduce token-gated attention to overcome this issue. Our method takes inspiration from Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022), which achieve sparsity over activated model parameters by gating expert sub-networks. We use similar form, but instead weight attention logits to achieve sparsity over processed tokens. Using this technique, we demonstrate that we can adapt existing trained models with cost similar to standard adaptation techniques. For instance, we can fine-tune existing models with TOKENGATE using simple next-tokenprediction loss, with no auxiliary loss and total train time similar to supervised fine-tuning on the base model. The resulting TOKENGATE model matches or exceeds accuracy over the trained base model, while significantly reducing prefill latency and memory. We evaluate TOKENGATE on diverse tasks, including code completion, multi-hop QA, multi-doc summarization, medical extraction, and needle-in-a-haystack, using both traditional transformer models and recent hybrid attention one. Overall, we show the following findings (1) TOKENGATE reduces TTFT and peak prefill memory by 1.4-11.3 and 1.5-3.4, respectively, at no accuracy degradation compared to the finetuned model baseline with full-context, and outperforms all training-free token pruning methods, by up to 6.4 faster prefill (TTFT) and 2 lower peak prefill memory relative to the next-best baseline, (2) TOKENGATE natively extends existing recent hybridattention architectures, like Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026), where it achieves 3.8 lower TTFT over the full-context baseline at no accuracy degradation, and 2.1 lower TTFT than the next best2 performing token-pruning method at fixed accuracy. (3) Training models is efficient with TOKENGATE, incurring minimal overhead compared to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques, like LoRA (Hu et al., 2021). Overall, we summarize our contributions as follows: We introduce TOKENGATE, small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning for fast and memory-efficient prefill. We propose token-gated attention, mechanism for training models end-to-end despite the gate modules non-differentiable top-K operator. Our systematic evaluation finds that TOKENGATE reduces TTFT and peak prefill memory by up to 6.4 and 2, respectively, compared to the next best-performing baselines, TOKENGATE natively extends transformer-based models, including recent hybrid-attention architectures. Further, training is efficient, with total train time comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Training-free Token Pruning. One body of prior work optimizes prefill using training-free tokenpruning methods (e.g., FastKV, SlimInfer, DASH, and GemFilter) (Jo et al., 2025; Long et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a; Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2021). These methods prune token hidden states at mid-layer of the model using attention-based heuristics to rank tokens, forwarding only the highest-scoring tokens to upper layers of the model. This body of work is closest to ours, however, unlike our work, these methods are not trainable. As we observe in (Section 5), these methods offer limited speedups before degrading accuracy because they employ heuristic attention-based token-ranking functions that under-perform our end-to-end trained scoring network, and they prevent co-adaptation of the model backbone with the pruning function, which our end-to-end trainable design enables. Architectural Modifications. Several lines of work explore architectural modifications to the selfattention-based transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), reducing the compute and memory of processing long-context inputs. First, one body of work studies architectures that achieve adaptive compute per token through dynamic token routing or learned pruning decisions, but are expensive to train. These works require pre-training from scratch (Dehghani et al., 2018; Bae et al., 2025; Graves, 2016; Raposo et al., 2024; Ainslie et al., 2023) or expensive fine-tuning with auxiliary loss terms that fix the token budget during train time, requiring re-training for each inference-time token budget (Kim et al., 2021; He et al., 2025; Goyal et al., 2020; Rao et al., 2021). In contrast to all of these works, TOKENGATE natively extends popular pre-trained language models and is simple and efficient to train. We show that with single fine-tuning pass, the resulting TOKENGATE model generalizes across input lengths and token budgets (Section 5, Appendix D.3). Other works on sub-quadratic architectures for language modeling introduce promising, new algorithms that reduce the per token compute and memory of attention operations, including new compute primitives and sparse attention mechanisms (Gu & Dao, 2023; Dao & Gu, 2024; Yang et al., 2024c;b; Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2024; Lai et al., 2025). However, unlike TOKENGATE, these architectures still process all tokens through each model layer. In Section 5 we demonstrate TOKENGATE natively extends recent hybrid architectures with subquadratic layers (Qwen Team, 2026), and enables even more efficient prefill. Conditional Computation. Mixture-of-experts layers achieve sparsity over the activated model parameters, making it possible to efficiently scale model capacity (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024). Our work is inspired by the success of this line of work, however, we focus on achieving sparsity over different axis, the input context length, for scalable long-context prefill. Decode Optimizations. large body of work targets the cost of decoding rather than prefill, evicting or merging KV-cache entries after prefill (Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2023; Ge et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025), and performing early exit or per-token routing for decoded tokens (Schuster et al., 2022; Elhoushi et al., 2024). These methods do not improve prefill efficiency and are complementary to prefill optimizations like ours. Detailed visualizations of real samples from all datasets are in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4 TRAINABLE TOKEN PRUNING WITH TOKENGATE
sections.content: TOKENGATE is drop-in neural network component, which places gate module within specified transformer layer1, L, to score and prune tokens, as shown in Figure 1. In this section, we describe how TOKENGATE enables trainable token pruning using two key components, the gate module (Section 4.1) and token-gated attention (Section 4.2). We will then overview an end-to-end training recipe for adapting existing models (Section 4.3). Overall, the full TOKENGATE forward pass with gating at layer decomposes into three phases. First, tokens pass through layers below the gate module, using standard forward pass. Second, the gate module processes all tokens, producing score for each, and selecting subset to prune. Third, the model performs pruned forward, processing only selected tokens in layers above the gate module, using token-gated attention, which re-weights attention scores using the importance scores. TOKENGATE reduces both the compute and memory footprint during prefill by preventing model layers after the gate module from processing pruned tokens or generating KV-cache entries for them.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: We evaluate the effectiveness of TOKENGATE on diverse tasks, including code completion, multihop QA, summarization, medical extraction, and needle-in-a-haystack. Overall, results demonstrate: TOKENGATE reduces TTFT and peak prefill memory by 1.4-11.3 and 1.5-3.4, respectively, at no accuracy degradation compared to the base model with full-context, and outperforms the next best-performing token pruning baselines by up to 6.4 and 2, respectively. TOKENGATE extends existing transformer-based models, including recent hybrid-attention architectures, achieving 3.8 lower TTFT than the full-context baseline at no accuracy degradation and 2.1 lower TTFT than the best prior methods, at fixed accuracy. Training models with TOKENGATE is efficient, incurring minimal training overhead, with total training time comparable to standard parameter efficient fine-tuning. We provide details of our experimental setup in Appendix C, additional experimental results including context-length extrapolation and ablations in Appendix D, and visualization in Appendix E. 2In practice, we sample from discrete list following this distribution for training efficiency with PyTorch compilation. 7 Datasets. We evaluate on five diverse tasks, including 3 LongBench datasets with available train sets (Bai et al., 2024), 2WikiMultihopQA (Ho et al., 2020), multi-hop QA dataset, RepoBenchP (Liu et al., 2023), next-line code completion dataset, and MultiNews (Fabbri et al., 2019), summarization dataset, as well as two additional tasks, BioDEXs drug-reaction extraction over biomedical papers (DOosterlinck et al., 2023) and needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) (Kamradt, 2023). We use the official evaluation metric for each. Baselines. We compare TOKENGATE against state-of-the-art token-pruning methods, FastKV (Jo et al., 2025), SlimInfer (Long et al., 2025), DASH (Chen et al., 2026), and GemFilter (Shi et al., 2024), as well as sparse attention methods, FlexPrefill (Lai et al., 2025) and MInference (Jiang et al., 2024). We run each baseline using fine-tuned base model trained to convergence with LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) (r=16). We train our model with TOKENGATE to convergence using the same LoRA configuration. We train both standard transformer model, Qwen3-1.7B (Yang et al., 2025), and hybrid architecture, Qwen3-2B (Qwen Team, 2026), each on 4 A100 GPUS.

sections.title: 5.1 FAST AND MEMORY-EFFICIENT PREFILL
sections.content: We evaluate the prefill efficiency of models trained with TOKENGATE. First, Figure 3 (top) shows the accuracy vs TTFT of each benchmarked method, demonstrating that across all datasets, the trained TOKENGATE model achieves pareto-optimal performance. Specifically, TOKENGATE reduces TTFT by 1.411.3 at no accuracy degradation compared to standard prefill, and by 1.26.4 compared to the next best-performing baseline. We measure FastKV, one of the best-performing baselines both at its default layer and at layer 1, the same layer index as the TOKENGATE. Notably, we observe that compared to FastKV (Layer 1), TOKENGATE significantly outperforms across all datasets, indicating the promise of end-to-end trainable token pruning for achieving prefill speedups. Turning our attention to the bottom row of Figure 3, we study the prefill memory footprint, reporting accuracy versus peak prefill memory. Once again, across all dataset, the TOKENGATE model establishes the Pareto-frontier, reducing peak memory by 1.53.4 compared to standard prefill at matched accuracy. Moreover the TOKENGATE model achieves up to 2.1 lower peak memory compared to the next best-performing baseline at matched accuracy. Overall, the results demonstrate that TOKENGATE significantly outperforms prior token-pruning methods, offering an exciting direction for improved prefill efficiency. 5.2 ABLATION STUDY: UNDERSTANDING THE PERFORMANCE OF TOKENGATE MODELS We hypothesize that TOKENGATE owes its superiority to end-to-end learnable token pruning. Our visualizations of the kept tokens for real samples (Appendix E) shows that TOKENGATE flexibly learns very different pruning patterns in task-dependent manner, ranging from keeping answer keywords for question answering to keeping stop-words at the ends of phrases for summarization (Figure 2). To understand this more rigorously, we investigate two key mechanisms: trainable tokenselection, and co-adaptation with the trained backbone. Trainable selector. First, to study the effectiveness of TOKENGATEs learned selector, we compare performance of the trained TOKENGATE model (Layer 1), to the same model with random token selection on 2WikiMultihopQA. Figure 5, demonstrates that the trained selector significantly outperforms the random-K selector on accuracy across all token budgets. Moreover, we compare against the FastKV selector applied at the same layer, Layer 1, of the finetuned base model. Notably, the TOKENGATE selector significantly outperforms the FastKV selector. This result demonstrates the value of an end-to-end trained gate module for token pruning: the trained scoring network leads to far better token selection compared to FastKV, which relies on heuristic using attention scores that offer only weak signal at early layers, resulting in accuracy degradation for aggressive pruning. Co-adaptation. Secondly, we analyze the effect of co-adaptation for TOKENGATE, which allows the model backbone and gate module to co-adapt. We compare the performance of random-K selection over the TOKENGATE model to the random-K selection over the finetuned base model. Notably, with the same random-K selector, the TOKENGATE model still outperforms the fine-tuned model, achieving higher accuracy across all token budgets, as Figure 5 shows. This result shows that TOKENGATEs end-to-end training allows the model to become more robust to token-pruning, likely redistributing information among tokens. 8 Figure 4: Accuracy vs. TTFT with the Qwen3.5-2B hybrid-attention architecture. Unlike TOKENGATE, FastKV can only prune at attention layers. Figure 5: F1 vs. kept context tokens on 2WikiMultihopQA with Qwen3-1.7B for gate and Random-K selection on the TOKENGATE model and FastKV and Random-K selection on the LoRA-trained model. Overall, the results show that end-to-end training with TOKENGATE enables state-of-the-art prefill performance through two complementary mechanism: the effectiveness of the learned scoring network, and co-adaptation, which allows the model to adapt jointly with the gating module for improved robustness to token pruning. 5.3 GENERALIZATION TO ALTERNATIVE ARCHITECTURES We evaluate how TOKENGATEs performance extends to recent hybrid-attention model, Qwen3.52B (Qwen Team, 2026) model, which uses full-attention layers every fourth layer and GatedDeltaNet (Yang et al., 2024b) for all other layer. We compare TOKENGATE against FastKV (Jo et al., 2025), the best-performing baseline in our main results (Section 5.1). We measure FastKV over the LoRA-tuned base model and the LoRA-tuned model with TOKENGATE, both at varying layers. FastKV uses an attention-based score function and natively applies only to full-attention layers (i.e., layer 3, 7, 11, etc). TOKENGATE natively extends both the full attention and GatedDeltaNet layers, so we apply it over both. We provide further details on TOKENGATE for Qwen3.5 in Appendix C.4. Figure 4 shows the accuracy vs TTFT of both methods at varying layers on the NIAH 32K dataset, demonstrating that TOKENGATEs strong performance extends to the hybrid-attention model. TOKENGATE (Layer 3) matches the accuracy of standard prefill at 3.8 lower TTFT, and 2.1 lower TTFT than the best-performing FastKV run at the same accuracy. Applying the TOKENGATE at the lower GatedDeltaNet layers (Layer 1,2) enable even higher TTFT reductions, up to 7.8 faster prefill, at accuracy within 6% of standard prefill, once again significantly outperforming FastKV. 5.4 GATE TRAINING EFFICIENCY We evaluate overhead of training models with TOKENGATE compared standard models, both with LoRA fine-tuning (r = 16). Table 2 in Appendix D.1 compares both, reporting total training time in A100 hours and the average per-step time during training for each evaluated dataset. Overall, we observe that TOKENGATE step is slower by 1.3 compared to the baseline due to its sampling at two token budgets per step. However, the TOKENGATE train runs converge after fewer steps on four of five tasks, leading to modestly reduced overall training time compared to the standard training.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we introduced TOKENGATE, neural network component that extends existing trained transformer models, enabling end-to-end trainable token pruning using token-gated attention. We demonstrate that that across diverse tasks, TOKENGATE reduces TTFT and peak prefill memory by up to 11.3 and 3.4, respectively, at no accuracy degradation compared to standard prefill, and by up to 6.4 and 2, respectively, compared to the best performing baselines. Crucially, TOKENGATE is compatible with diverse transformer-based architectures, is simple to train, and incurs minimal training overhead, making it promising drop-in replacement for standard fine-tuning over trained backbones. In the future, we envision models trained with TOKENGATE will enable broad range of applications, including medical extraction, deep research, and coding agents, where processing long-context inputs is critical, but currently prohibitively expensive.

sections.title: A EFFICIENT KERNELS FOR TOKENGATE
sections.content: i Token-gated attention (Eq. 8) differs from standard causal attention in two ways: per-query temperature τ ℓh and per-key, per-head gate term added to the attention logits. The temperature is applied by scaling each query before the attention call, so it needs no kernel support. The gate term needs per-key bias, which standard fused kernels do not accept, and unfused or score-modifying kernels are substantially slower. We therefore patch FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023) to read per-key, per-head bias vector, which it adds to each tile of attention scores before the online softmax. This keeps the fused structure of the kernel: the bias adds one vector load per key block, and biased call costs 1.01.1 plain one. The kernel supports head dimensions 128 (Qwen3) and 256 (Qwen3.5). Training. The same kernel provides the backward pass: the gradient of the bias of key is the sum over queries of the gradient of its attention scores, which the kernel accumulates alongside the usual gradients, so the task loss reaches the scoring network through the fused kernel. The two targets of each training step (Eq. 10) are packed into one variable-length call. For Qwen3.5, whose Gated DeltaNet layers are not supported by this path, we train with FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2024) and add the bias as score modification, but more optimized kernels are possible. Inference. Layers at and below the gate use the standard fused kernel (cuDNN on A100). The pruned forward of the post-gate layers is captured as one CUDA graph per padded length: the kept sequence is padded to multiple of 64, and pad keys receive bias of 109 so the result is exact. The gather of the KV cache of layers ℓ to the kept tokens (Appendix B) runs on separate stream, concurrently with the post-gate layers. During decoding, the gate term of each kept key is fixed, so it is folded once into an additive attention mask per post-gate layer and decoding uses standard attention.

sections.title: B DECODING WITH TOKENGATE
sections.content: The layers above the gate, ℓ > L, never compute KV entries for pruned tokens, so during decoding each new token attends there only to the kept tokens and the tokens generated so far. The layers at and below the gate, ℓ L, process the full context during prefill, so by default their KV cache holds every context token, and decode tokens attend to the full context in these layers and to the pruned context above them. Optionally, TOKENGATE can also prune the cache of layers ℓ L. In the post-gate layers, decode tokens use the same token-gated softmax as prefill (Eq. 8). The gate term softplus(γℓh) bj of each kept key is computed once at prefill and stored with the cache as constant per-key bias, and each generated token is non-prunable token with gate term 0 (Eq. 3). The temperature τ ℓh of decode query follows Eq. 7, with mi its rank among the kept and generated tokens and pi its original position; generated tokens continue from the original position of the last prompt token.

sections.title: C DETAILS OF EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: C.1 DATASETS All datasets are evaluated on Qwen3-1.7B with greedy decoding for up to 1024 new tokens. Each model is fine-tuned on training set that is disjoint from its evaluation set. RepoBench-P. RepoBench-P (Liu et al., 2023) is next-line code completion task. We use the LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) version, whose prompts contain cross-file code context and an in-file prefix, and the model completes the next line. We evaluate on all 500 samples (mean context 11.0k tokens, up to 39k) and report edit similarity, 1 Levenshtein/ max(length), on the first generated line. For training, we use 14.9k samples from the RepoBench v1.1 Python and Java cross-file splits, deduplicated against the evaluation set. 2WikiMultihopQA. 2WikiMultihopQA (Ho et al., 2020) is multi-hop question answering task over several Wikipedia passages; we use the LongBench version. We evaluate on all 200 samples (mean context 7.5k tokens) and report token-level F1 against the gold answers. For training, we use 20k 2WikiMultihopQA questions with contexts rebuilt from full Wikipedia articles and decontaminated against LongBench. 16 MultiNews. MultiNews (Fabbri et al., 2019) is multi-document news summarization task; we use the LongBench version. We evaluate on all 200 samples (mean context 2.7k tokens, up to 14k) and report ROUGE-L. For training, we use 44.8k samples from the MultiNews training split in the LongBench prompt format. BioDEX. BioDEX-Reactions (DOosterlinck et al., 2023) is an adverse drug reaction extraction task over full-text biomedical papers: given paper, the model lists the reported adverse reactions as MedDRA terms. We evaluate on 500 samples drawn from the official validation split with articles between 2k and 39k tokens (mean 4.5k), and report set F1 between predicted and gold reactions, counting predicted reaction as correct if it matches gold term up to substring containment. For training, we use 9.8k papers from the official training split. NIAH. NIAH (Kamradt, 2023) is needle-in-a-haystack retrieval at 16k tokens. The haystack is built from Paul Graham essays, and the needle, The best thing to do in city is activity., is inserted at sentence boundary at given depth; the model is then asked for the best thing to do in that city. The 200 evaluation samples cover 20 held-out cities at 10 depths evenly spaced from 0 to 1, and we report accuracy, i.e., whether the gold activity appears in the answer. For training, we use 12k generated samples with haystacks of 14k16.4k tokens and uniformly random depths; the essays and cities are disjoint from the evaluation set. C.2 BASELINES All baselines run on the same SFT model, fine-tuned on each dataset with LoRA (r=16, α=32) on the query and value projections of all layers. The pruning baselines keep all non-document tokens and prune only document tokens, with the same kept-token budgets as TOKENGATE (648192). We briefly describe each baseline below, and the configurations used. We run each method, applying its optimization for prefill-only. FastKV (Jo et al., 2025). At token-selective propagation layer, FastKV scores tokens by the attention they receive from window of the last queries, max-pools the scores, and propagates only the top-K tokens to deeper layers. We use the papers observation window of 8 tokens and pooling kernel of 7. We run it at layer 13 by default, following the paper and its hyper-parameter search, which chooses relative depth of 46% for its models. We additionally run the baseline at layer 1, the layer at which we apply TOKENGATE, to compare performance at matched layer index. SlimInfer (Long et al., 2025). SlimInfer prunes hidden states in several stages: at layers 8, 17 and 25 it keeps 3K, 1.5K and tokens, scoring 64-token blocks by the attention of the last 4 queries. We use the papers block size, kernel and layer schedule, and its budget ratios, following the papers hyperparameter search. GemFilter (Shi et al., 2024). GemFilter runs the first layers on the full prompt, selects the top-K tokens by the last querys attention scores at filter layer, and then runs fresh forward pass over only the selected tokens. We use filter layer 12, at the same relative depth (0.4) as recommended by the original paper, and the official pooling kernel. DASH (Chen et al., 2026). DASH halts tokens whose representations have stabilized: at layer 11 (0.4 the number of layers, the official default), it ranks tokens by the change in their hidden state from the previous layer and drops the most stable ones, keeping document tokens. FlexPrefill (Lai et al., 2025). FlexPrefill is sparse-attention method: it keeps all tokens but computes query-adaptive sparse attention pattern during prefill, controlled by cumulative-attention threshold γ. We use the official kernel and its recommended hyperparameters (divergence threshold τ =0.1, which decides per head whether to use query-aware or vertical-slash pattern; minimum budget 1024; block size 128) and sweep γ {0.1, 0.2, . . . , 0.9, 0.95, 0.97}, extending the range until accuracy degrades. MInference (Jiang et al., 2024). MInference uses per-head sparse attention patterns found by an offline search, which for Qwen3-1.7B selects vertical-and-slash patterns for all heads. We run the official implementation with patterns searched on Qwen3-1.7B, and sweep its budget by scaling the vertical and slash sizes of the searched configuration by {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, which keeps the searched pattern shape. 17 Implementation and timing. All methods run the same fine-tuned backbone in bf16 with the LoRA adapter folded into the weights, and all dense decoder layers are torch.compiled. Dense causal attention uses the same fused kernel in every lane (cuDNN on the A100; FlashAttention-2 on Qwen3.5-2B); the only kernel that differs is in the TOKENGATEs post-gate layers, which require per-key bias and use FlashAttention-2 variant at 1.01.1 the cost of plain call (Appendix A). FastKV and GemFilter run through the compiled layers directly. The official SlimInfer and DASH prefills bypass the compiled layer forward, so we reimplemented both in compile-friendly form and verified that they select the same tokens as the official code (DASH bit-identical; SlimInfer identical selection), which made them 1.22.4 and 1.251.56 faster; we report the faster versions. MInference is compiled around its sparse kernel with identical accuracy, and FlexPrefill runs eager, its fastest configuration, since its data-dependent block selection triggers recompilation under torch.compile. The pruned forward of the TOKENGATE and of FastKV is captured as one CUDA graph per padded length; the remaining baselines have no fixed-shape pruned phase to capture. Both FastKV and the TOKENGATE optionally prune the KV cache of the layers below their pruning layer to the selected tokens once prefill completes, so that decoding holds entries at every layer; we disable this setting for both in all experiments since KV cache pruning presents an orthogonal set of optimizations and our experiments instead isolate the effect of token pruning for prefill optimization (Appendix B). Inference timings are measured at batch size of 1 on one A100. C.3 TRAINING HYPERPARAMETERS Table 1 lists the hyperparameters used to train the TOKENGATE models and the SFT baseline on each dataset. Both use the same LoRA configuration, learning rate, schedule and training data; they differ only in the optimizer of the TOKENGATE parameters and in the token budgets sampled during training. C.4 EXTENSION TO ALTERNATIVE HYBRID-ATTENTION ARCHITECTURES Qwen3.5 architecture. Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026) is hybrid-attention model with 24 layers. Every fourth layer, ℓ = {3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23}, is full-attention layer whose output is multiplied by learned sigmoid output gate. All other layers are Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2024b), which replace softmax attention with linear recurrence over fixed-size state and therefore have no attention weights. Gate module. We place the TOKENGATE at layer {1, 2, 3}, where layers 1 and 2 are Gated DeltaNet layers and layer 3 is the first full-attention layer. The scoring network (Eq. 3) and the top-K selector (Eq. 4) are unchanged. The only difference is the token mixer of layer L: the scoring network reads the normalized residual after layer Ls mixer, aL = LN (cid:0)hL + MixerL(LN1(hL))j (cid:1), MixerL {GatedDeltaNetL, AttnL}, (11) which for Gated DeltaNet layer is the output of its recurrence rather than of self-attention. 18 Token-gated attention. Since Gated DeltaNet layers have no attention logits to bias, token-gated attention (Eq. 8), including the gains γℓh and the temperature, is applied only in the full-attention layers above the gate, ℓ A, ℓ > L. The Gated DeltaNet layers above the gate run unchanged on the kept tokens S, starting from an empty state, so that their recurrent state is built from the kept tokens only: hℓ = (cid:26)token-gated attention layer (Eq. 8) GatedDeltaNetℓ (cid:0)hℓ (cid:1) ℓ A, ℓ > L, ℓ / A, ℓ > L. The recurrent state of Gated DeltaNet layer summarizes all tokens it has seen in fixed-size matrix and cannot be pruned per token. The Gated DeltaNet layers ℓ therefore decode from state built over the full prompt, while the KV cache of full-attention layers are pruned, as in Appendix B. Training. As for Qwen3, we train the TOKENGATE jointly with LoRA (r=16) on the query and value projections, which in Qwen3.5 exist only in the full-attention layers; the Gated DeltaNet layers are not adapted.

Meanwhile, the peak memory reduction is consistent across all length ranges, as expected, since peak memory is dominated by memory footprint of the standard forward that occurs without pruning in layers below the gate. D.4 ABLATING THE TOKENGATE DESIGN In this section we ablate the TOKENGATE design (Section 4). First, Figure 7 (left) compares the accuracy vs TTFT performance of TOKENGATE on BioDEX with Qwen3-1.7B against three variants: (a) removing the full-context loss term LKfull from the per-step loss (Eq. 10), (b) removing the temperature scaling term during token-gated attention, and (c) removing the head-wise scaling. The results demonstrate that training without the full-context loss most significantly degrades inference accuracy at full-context, and removing the temperature scaling and head-wise gain also degrades accuracy, leading to sub-optimal accuracy vs TTFT. We additionally analyze layer selection, hyperparameter for TOKENGATE. Figure 7 (right) shows performance on BioDEX of Qwen3-1.7B models trained with the TOKENGATE at Layer 0, 1, and 2. Notably, the model with gating at Layer 0 is Pareto-suboptimal relative to the Layer 1 and 2 gate models, suggesting that the Layer 0 post-attention residuals provide insufficient signal for the TOKENGATE scoring network. On the other hand, the Layer 1 and Layer 2 TOKENGATE models both lie along the Pareto frontier, suggesting that by Layer 1, the post-attention residuals passed to the gate module are sufficiently rich to learn an effective scoring network for trainable token pruning.
